g9-history-uh3-t1.overview: Ethiopia and the Horn are home to more than eighty languages and to four major religious traditions. This lesson classifies the peoples of the region by language super-family and explains how Christianity and Islam entered the region.
objectives: Describe the two major language super-families of Ethiopia and the Horn
Classify the Cushitic, Semitic, Omotic, Chari-Nile and Koman language families
Explain how Christianity was introduced and expanded in Ethiopia
Analyse how Islam entered the Horn through the Red Sea, Zeila and the Indian Ocean
Discuss indigenous religion and the place of the Bete-Israel in Ethiopian history
g9-history-uh3-t1.simple: Ethiopia and the Horn contain great ethnic and linguistic diversity: more than eighty languages with many dialects are spoken, yet the peoples share a strong unity. Linguists group these languages into two super-families, Afro-Asiatic and Nilo-Saharan. Afro-Asiatic has Cushitic, Semitic and Omotic families; Nilo-Saharan has Chari-Nile and Koman. The major religions are indigenous religion, Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Indigenous faiths believe in one Supreme Being while revering natural powers, and where these beliefs mix with the newer faiths the result is called syncretism. Christianity reached Aksum around 330 AD through Frumentius, who converted King Ezana, and Islam arrived peacefully from 615 AD when Muslim refugees found asylum in Aksum.
g9-history-uh3-t1.detailed:
A land of many languages. Ethiopia and the Horn are marked by ethnic and linguistic diversity. More than eighty languages with many dialects are spoken there, yet the peoples share a strong unity that goes beyond cultural and linguistic difference. Linguists classify these languages into two major super-families: Afro-Asiatic and Nilo-Saharan.

The Afro-Asiatic super-family. This super-family covers the largest sector of the population and is divided into three families: Cushitic, Semitic and Omotic. Cushitic speakers form the vast majority in terms of both area and numbers, and Cushitic has North, Central and Eastern branches. North Cushitic is represented only by Beja in north-western Eritrea. Central Cushitic is represented by Bilen in Eritrea and by the Agaw languages such as Qimant, Himitagna and Awign. Eastern Cushitic is the largest and most diverse branch, split into Highland and Lowland groups. Lowland East Cushitic includes Oromo, Afar, Somali, Konso, Gidole, Erbore, Dassenech and Saho, while Highland East Cushitic includes Hadiya, Kambata, Tambaro, Halaba, Sidama, Gedeo and Burji.

Semitic and Omotic. Semitic is divided into Northern and Southern groups. Northern Semitic includes Geez, the ancient language of northern Ethiopia now used in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, together with Tigrigna and Tegra. Southern Semitic includes Amharic, Argobba, Gafat (now extinct), Guraghigna, Siltie, Harari and Zay. Omotic speakers live mostly in and around the Omo River basin and include Ari, Banna, Bench, Dawuro, Gamo, Wolaita and Keficho; the Shinasha in Benishangul-Gumuz and Anfillo in Wallaga show how far the family once spread.

The Nilo-Saharan super-family. In Ethiopia these peoples live mainly on the Ethio-Sudanese border, although some live in the Abay gorge and along the tributaries of the Abay in Wallaga. The super-family has two families. Chari-Nile includes Anuak, Nuer, Mien, Majang, Benishangul, Kunama, Mursi, Surma and Tirma. Koman includes Gumuz, Koma, Sese, Mao and Komo. Several languages are extinct or in danger of extinction because their speakers are decreasing; Gafat is an example of a language that has disappeared.

Indigenous religion. The major religions of Ethiopia are indigenous religion, Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Indigenous religions are practised only within a given culture and are native to the region. Sedentary settlement and agricultural development produced priests who prayed for rainfall, thanksgiving and safety from natural hazards, and farmers paid them tribute. Followers believe in one Supreme Being while attributing special power to natural phenomena considered sacred. The Waqeffanna of the Oromo worships Waqa, revealed through the spirits called Ayyana; the revered experts Qallu (male) and Qallitti (female) keep the link between the Ayyana and the believers. Where indigenous beliefs mix with Christianity or Islam the result is called syncretism.

Judaism and Christianity. Judaism has been practised since ancient times by the Bete-Israel, literally house of Israel, who lived in north-western Ethiopia before most of the community moved to Israel in the 1980s and 1990s. Christianity was introduced around 330 AD by Frumentius, also called Freminatos, who converted King Ezana (r. 320-350 AD). With royal support it became the state religion and expanded further when the Nine Saints arrived at the end of the fifth century; the first monastery was Debre-Damo and the Bible was translated into Geez. Patriarch Atnatewos of Alexandria consecrated Frumentius as Abuna Salam, the first bishop, and bishops continued to come from Egypt until 1959, when Abune Baselios became the first Ethiopian Patriarch.

Islam. Islam arose in the early seventh century in the Arabian Peninsula. In 615 AD, when the Quraysh tribe persecuted his followers, Prophet Mohammed sent a small group led by Jafar Abu Talib to Aksum, where King Armah Ella Seham (Ahmed al-Nejash in Arabic sources) gave them asylum from 615 to 628. Because of this welcome the Prophet exempted Aksum from jihad. Islam then entered the Horn by peaceful means through three gateways: the Red Sea in the north, the Gulf of Aden in the east and the Indian Ocean in the southeast. After Adulis was destroyed in 702 AD and Muslim Arabs occupied the Dahlak Islands, the port of Zeila grew in importance and carried Islam into eastern Harar, Shewa and Wollo and later into Bale, Arsi and Hadya, while coastal towns such as Mogadishu, Brava and Merca carried it into the Somali region.

keyTerms.def: The broadest grouping of related languages; Ethiopia and the Horn have two, Afro-Asiatic and Nilo-Saharan.
The Afro-Asiatic family spoken by the largest number of people in Ethiopia and the Horn, divided into North, Central and Eastern branches.
The Afro-Asiatic family of northern Ethiopian languages such as Geez, Tigrigna and Amharic.
An Afro-Asiatic family whose speakers live mostly in and around the Omo River basin.
The second super-family, spoken mainly on the Ethio-Sudanese border and divided into Chari-Nile and Koman.
Literally house of Israel; the community that kept the Jewish faith in north-western Ethiopia.
The indigenous religion of the Oromo, based on one Supreme Being called Waqa revealed through spirits called Ayyana.
The mixing of religious beliefs and practices, for example when indigenous customs are fused with Christianity or Islam.

workedExamples.problem: Classify Somali, Amharic, Wolaita and Gumuz by language family and super-family.
workedExamples.given: Somali is a Lowland East Cushitic language, Amharic is Southern Semitic, Wolaita belongs to Ometo within Omotic, and Gumuz is Koman.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: every language of Ethiopia belongs to a super-family (Afro-Asiatic or Nilo-Saharan), a family and often a branch.
workedExamples.substitution: Cushitic, Semitic and Omotic are families of Afro-Asiatic; Koman is a family of Nilo-Saharan.
workedExamples.calculation: Somali and Wolaita are Afro-Asiatic (Cushitic and Omotic), Amharic is Afro-Asiatic (Semitic), while Gumuz is Nilo-Saharan.
workedExamples.answer: Somali: Afro-Asiatic, Cushitic, Lowland East. Amharic: Afro-Asiatic, Semitic. Wolaita: Afro-Asiatic, Omotic. Gumuz: Nilo-Saharan, Koman.

workedExamples.problem: Why did Islam spread into the interior through Zeila but fail to penetrate the northern highlands?
workedExamples.given: Adulis was destroyed in 702 AD, Arab Muslims occupied the Dahlak Islands, and the Zeila route linked the port with the interior. Christianity had been established in the highlands since the mid-fourth century AD.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: religion spreads along trade routes unless an established rival faith already controls the region.
workedExamples.substitution: The Zeila route reached Harar, Shewa, Wollo and later Bale, Arsi and Hadya, while the northern highlands were already Christian.
workedExamples.calculation: Trade carried Islam inland in the south and east, but in the north a strong Christian state blocked it, so Islam stayed in the coastal lowlands.
workedExamples.answer: Islam followed the Zeila trade route into the interior; in the north it was confined to the lowlands because Christianity was already well established in the highlands.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why Gafat is described as extinct but other Ethiopian languages are only in danger of extinction.
workedExamples.given: Gafat, a Southern Semitic language, has no speakers left, whereas other languages still have small and decreasing numbers of speakers.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: a language dies when its last speakers stop transmitting it to the next generation.
workedExamples.substitution: Extinction means the number of speakers has reached zero, while endangerment means the number is falling.
workedExamples.calculation: Gafat reached zero speakers, so it is extinct; languages with few but surviving speakers are in danger of extinction.
workedExamples.answer: Gafat is extinct because it has no speakers left, while other languages are only endangered because a small number of speakers remains.

commonMistakes: Thinking all Ethiopian languages belong to a single family, instead of two super-families and several families.
Believing Cushitic languages are all found in one place, when the family spreads across the highlands and lowlands.
Assuming Omotic speakers live only near the Omo River, ignoring the Shinasha in Benishangul-Gumuz and Anfillo in Wallaga.
Confusing indigenous religion, which is native to a culture, with the world religions of Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
Believing Islam reached Ethiopia by force, when it entered through peaceful trade routes after the refugees were welcomed in 615 AD.
Assuming Geez is still a daily spoken language, when it is now used mainly in the Orthodox Church.
applications: Recognising the language family of a neighbour's mother tongue and treating it with respect.
Drawing a simple map that shows where Cushitic, Semitic, Omotic and Nilo-Saharan speakers live.
Tracing on a map how Islam spread from the port of Zeila into the interior along trade routes.
Explaining to a friend why Ethiopia's diversity of language and religion is a source of unity.
Visiting a local church, mosque or shrine and describing its place in the community's history.
Reading an inscription or a manuscript and identifying whether it uses Geez, Greek or Sabean.
g9-history-uh3-t1.summary: Ethiopia and the Horn speak more than eighty languages that belong to the Afro-Asiatic and Nilo-Saharan super-families, with the Cushitic family being the largest. The major religions are indigenous religion, Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Christianity arrived around 330 AD through Frumentius, who converted King Ezana, while Islam entered peacefully from 615 AD and later spread inland along the Zeila trade route. Diversity of language and faith has not prevented the peoples of the region from sharing a common history.

g9-history-uh3-t2.overview: Before Aksum rose, a series of states already flourished in the Horn and traded with Egypt and South Arabia. This lesson introduces Punt, Yeha, Hawlti-Melazo, Addi-Seglemeni, Metera, Kaskase and Damat and explains the geographical setting that allowed them to grow.
objectives: Describe the location and trade of the state of Punt
List the pre-Aksumite states that emerged from about 1000 BC
Explain the achievements of Yeha and Hawlti-Melazo
Analyse Damat's links with South Arabia and the port of Adulis
Evaluate how geography and trade shaped the earliest states of the Horn
g9-history-uh3-t2.simple: Long before Aksum, other states existed in Ethiopia and the Horn. The oldest known was Punt, whose exact borders are unknown but whose land lay along the Red Sea and Indian Ocean coasts of present-day Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia. Egyptian records show that Punt traded with Egypt since the third millennium BC, sending gold, ivory, skins, myrrh and ostrich feathers. From about 1000 BC other centres appeared, including Yeha, Hawlti-Melazo, Addi-Seglemeni, Metera, Kaskase and Coloe. Yeha, about 30 km north-east of Aksum, was the oldest and its wealth peaked between 750 and 500 BC. Damat, whose centre lay south of Aksum, used the port of Adulis and its rulers took the South Arabian title Mukarib.
g9-history-uh3-t2.detailed:
Punt. Punt was an ancient and historically known state in the Horn of Africa, although its exact location and territorial limits are not well known. Historians place its territory in the Red Sea and Indian Ocean coastal parts of present-day Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia. An Egyptian hieroglyphic states that the land of Punt lay south of Egypt and had trade relations with Egypt since the third millennium BC, carried on by land and sea routes.

What Punt traded. Egyptian inscriptions and pictorial reliefs indicate the objects that Punt supplied to Egypt. These exports originated in the interior that later became Ethiopia and the Horn. They include gold from the Ethiopian interior, mainly western Ethiopia, as well as ivory, panther and other skins, myrrh and myrrh trees and ostrich feathers. In return the Egyptians sent hatchets, daggers and necklaces. This exchange shows that the early states of the region were already linked to the wider world of the Nile and the Red Sea.

Other pre-Aksumite states. Further pre-Aksumite states emerged from about 1000 BC. These include Yeha, Hawlti-Melazo, Addi-Seglemeni, Metera, Kaskase and Coloe.

Yeha. Yeha is located about 30 kilometres north-east of Aksum and was the oldest of these centres, presumably first appearing around 1000 BC. Its wealth peaked between 750 and 500 BC. The remains of the walls of some of its buildings, its stone masonry, a still-standing temple and its inscriptions all indicate the glory of Yeha.

Hawlti-Melazo and Damat. Hawlti-Melazo is situated to the south-east of Aksum, where inscribed stone tablets have been excavated. Damat existed before the rise of Aksum, with its centre a few kilometres south of Aksum. Its rulers adopted the South Arabian political and religious title Mukarib, and Damat appears to have established external relations with South Arabia, as a local inscription left by one of its rulers in the fifth century BC shows. Damat used the Red Sea coast port of Adulis.

Why the geographical setting mattered. These states sat between the Ethiopian interior, rich in gold and other goods, and the Red Sea coast. That position allowed Punt and, later, Yeha, Hawlti-Melazo and Damat to trade with Egypt and South Arabia, so geography and trade, not conquest alone, explain how the earliest states of the region grew. The old belief that Aksum was the first centralised polity in Ethiopia and the Horn is therefore no longer accepted, because several principalities emerged and declined before it.

keyTerms.def: An ancient state of the Horn of Africa known from Egyptian records since the third millennium BC, whose exact location is not certain.
States that emerged before the rise of Aksum, such as Yeha, Hawlti-Melazo, Addi-Seglemeni, Metera, Kaskase and Damat.
The oldest of the post-1000 BC centres, about 30 km north-east of Aksum, whose wealth peaked between 750 and 500 BC.
A centre south-east of Aksum where inscribed stone tablets have been excavated.
A pre-Aksumite state with its centre a few kilometres south of Aksum, whose rulers used the title Mukarib and the port of Adulis.
A South Arabian political and religious title adopted by the rulers of Damat.
The Red Sea coast port used by Damat and later the main trade outlet of Aksum.
A form of Egyptian writing whose inscriptions and reliefs record Punt and its trade with Egypt.

workedExamples.problem: Which state in the region formed first, Punt or Yeha? Justify your answer with dates.
workedExamples.given: Punt had trade relations with Egypt since the third millennium BC; Yeha first appeared around 1000 BC and peaked between 750 and 500 BC.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: to place states in order, compare the earliest dates given by sources for each.
workedExamples.substitution: The third millennium BC is much earlier than 1000 BC.
workedExamples.calculation: Punt is attested from the third millennium BC, while Yeha appears only around 1000 BC, so Punt is the earlier state.
workedExamples.answer: Punt came first; the Egyptian record reaches back to the third millennium BC, well before Yeha.

workedExamples.problem: Using the goods exchanged, explain what the Punt trade reveals about the economy of the Ethiopian interior.
workedExamples.given: Punt sent gold, ivory, panther and other skins, myrrh and myrrh trees and ostrich feathers; Egypt sent hatchets, daggers and necklaces.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: exports show a region's natural wealth, while imports show the technology and crafts it lacked.
workedExamples.substitution: Gold and skins come from the interior, while hatchets and daggers are manufactured tools.
workedExamples.calculation: Because Punt exported raw materials and imported finished tools, the interior was rich in resources but depended on Egypt for metal tools.
workedExamples.answer: The interior was rich in gold and animal products but looked to Egypt for manufactured goods such as tools and ornaments.

workedExamples.problem: Why is an inscription left by a Damat ruler important evidence for historians?
workedExamples.given: One ruler of Damat left a local inscription in the fifth century BC, and the rulers used the South Arabian title Mukarib.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: a primary source produced in the period is stronger evidence than later tradition.
workedExamples.substitution: The inscription is a contemporary document, not a later story.
workedExamples.calculation: A local inscription of the fifth century BC directly proves Damat's external relations with South Arabia.
workedExamples.answer: It is a primary source that proves Damat had contact with South Arabia and borrowed its title Mukarib in the fifth century BC.

commonMistakes: Assuming Aksum was the very first state in the region, when Punt and other principalities came before it.
Thinking the exact borders of Punt are known, when its location and territorial limits are not well known.
Mixing up the goods Punt exported with those Egypt sent in return.
Placing Yeha later than Aksum instead of about 1000 BC.
Confusing Hawlti-Melazo, which lies south-east of Aksum, with Yeha, which lies north-east of Aksum.
Forgetting that Damat used the port of Adulis, which later served Aksum.
applications: Marking the approximate coastal area of Punt on a map of the Horn of Africa.
Reading an Egyptian relief as a primary source and listing the goods it shows.
Comparing the achievements of Yeha and Damat in a short written report.
Explaining why a state located between a rich interior and a sea coast tends to grow through trade.
Visiting or researching a local archaeological site to learn how historians use ruins and inscriptions.
g9-history-uh3-t2.summary: Punt was the earliest known state of the Horn, trading with Egypt since the third millennium BC, and from about 1000 BC centres such as Yeha, Hawlti-Melazo, Addi-Seglemeni, Metera, Kaskase and Damat emerged. Yeha was the oldest of these and its wealth peaked between 750 and 500 BC, while Damat adopted the South Arabian title Mukarib and used the port of Adulis. Geography and trade, not Aksum alone, explain how the first states of the region arose.

g9-history-uh3-t3.overview: Aksum emerged in the first century AD and became one of the great civilisations of the ancient world, expanding from southern Arabia to the Abay. This lesson explains its rise, its economy, its written language, its religion and the causes of its decline.
objectives: Describe the rise and territorial expansion of the Aksumite Kingdom
Explain the nature of the Aksumite economy and society
Analyse the role of Geez, Greek and Sabean in Aksumite culture
Evaluate the factors that caused the decline of Aksum
Appreciate the place of Ethiopia among the great civilisations of the world
g9-history-uh3-t3.simple: Aksum appeared in the first century AD with its nucleus at the city of Aksum, which served as its political and religious centre and was adorned with temples and tall stone steles. At first a small state, it expanded between the fourth and sixth centuries to reach southern Arabia in the east, the Abay in the west, the northern tip of Eritrea in the north and north Shewa in the south. Its people lived by plough agriculture, paid tribute to the king and grew rich from trade through the port of Adulis, using coins of bronze, silver and gold. Geez became a written language in the first three centuries, and the Aksumites followed indigenous religions before Christianity arrived in the fourth century. Decline began when the Red Sea passed under Muslim Arab control and Adulis was destroyed in 702 AD.
g9-history-uh3-t3.detailed:
The rise of Aksum. In the pre-Aksumite period Aksum was not the first state to emerge in Ethiopia. Aksum appeared in the first century AD with its nucleus at Aksum, and the city served as its political and religious centre. It was adorned with several temples and stone monuments such as the monolithic steles of Aksum.

Territorial expansion. Initially Aksum was a small state. Between the fourth and sixth centuries, Aksumite kings expanded the kingdom significantly to include territories bounded by the Red Sea and southern Arabia in the east, the River Abay in the west, the northern tip of Eritrea in the north and north Shewa in the south.

Economy and society. Economically, the Aksumites depended on plough agriculture, and Aksum was a powerful state with a well-demarcated social structure. The link between the king and the people was the payment of tribute. The state also generated considerable income from local and external trade conducted through the port of Adulis on the Red Sea coast. To facilitate trade, coins of bronze, silver and gold were minted.

Language and religion. In the first three centuries Geez evolved as a written language. Inscriptions and coins show that Sabean and Greek languages were used in Aksum before Geez; the use of Greek probably resulted from trade contact with the Greco-Roman world, since Greek was the lingua franca of the Red Sea and the Mediterranean region at that time. The Aksumites followed indigenous religions before the introduction of Christianity in the fourth century AD and the appearance of Islam in the early seventh century.

Civilisation and legacy. Unlike many other centres of civilisation such as Yeha, Metera and Adulis, Aksum continued to exist as the most important centre of a highly developed civilisation for several centuries. This is attested by the ruins of Aksumite temples, iron tools, bricks, coins, tombs and obelisks. Shipbuilding technology was also well known in the port town of Adulis. As a result, these ruins have become among the best-known tourist centres in Ethiopia today.

Decline. Gradually, Aksum deteriorated. The process began when the Red Sea came under the control of Muslim Arabs and the port of Adulis was destroyed in 702 AD. The loss of trade led to the decline of Aksum's economic, political and military power. Internally, rebellion broke out against King Kaleb (r. 500-535 AD), who had once controlled South Arabia in 525 AD, but the South Arabians finally expelled the Aksumite governors and soldiers between 580 and 590 AD, so Aksum lost control of the trade on the other side of the Red Sea. Internal political disturbances continued, and finally, unable to check the rebellions of the Beja people in the north, the Aksumite state was pushed southward to Kubar in southern Tigray and by the late ninth century it had taken refuge in the area predominantly inhabited by the Agaw people.

keyTerms.def: The kingdom that emerged in the first century AD with its nucleus at the city of Aksum, its political and religious centre.
A tall monolithic stone monument that adorned the city of Aksum.
The payment that linked the king and the people in the Aksumite state.
The Red Sea port through which Aksum earned much of its income from external trade.
The written language that evolved in Aksum during the first three centuries AD, later used in the Orthodox Church.
A common language used between speakers of different tongues; Greek played this role in the Red Sea region.
The place in southern Tigray to which the Aksumite state was pushed as it declined.
A people of the north whose rebellions the Aksumite state could not finally check.

workedExamples.problem: Explain how Aksum changed from a state based on agriculture to one based on trade.
workedExamples.given: The Aksumites depended on plough agriculture and tribute at first, but later local and external trade through Adulis became a primary source of income, and coins of bronze, silver and gold were minted.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: a state's main source of income can shift when a valuable trade route comes under its control.
workedExamples.substitution: The port of Adulis connected the Ethiopian interior to Red Sea and Mediterranean markets.
workedExamples.calculation: As trade through Adulis grew, it generated income alongside agriculture, and coins were minted to ease that trade, so the economy became trade-based as well as agricultural.
workedExamples.answer: Aksum remained agricultural but the Red Sea trade through Adulis became its primary source of income, supported by minted coins.

workedExamples.problem: Why is the use of Greek in Aksum evidence of contact with the wider world?
workedExamples.given: Inscriptions and coins show that Sabean and Greek were used in Aksum before Geez, and Greek was the lingua franca of the Red Sea and the Mediterranean.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: the languages on coins and inscriptions reveal the trading partners of a state.
workedExamples.substitution: Greek links Aksum to the Greco-Roman world and Sabean links it to South Arabia.
workedExamples.calculation: Because Greek was the common trade language of the region, its use proves Aksum traded with the Greco-Roman world before Geez replaced it.
workedExamples.answer: It shows that Aksum was in active trade contact with the Greco-Roman world, which used Greek as the common language of commerce.

workedExamples.problem: Identify the main cause of the decline of Aksum and explain its consequences.
workedExamples.given: The Red Sea came under Muslim Arab control and Adulis was destroyed in 702 AD, while internal rebellion and Beja attacks weakened the state.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: loss of a key trade route damages a state's economic, political and military power at the same time.
workedExamples.substitution: Adulis was the main outlet of Aksumite external trade.
workedExamples.calculation: With Adulis destroyed, trade income fell; without money the state could not pay for defence or control its regions, so it was pushed south to Kubar and then into Agaw country.
workedExamples.answer: The main cause was the loss of the Red Sea trade after Adulis fell in 702 AD, which undermined Aksum's power and forced it southward.

commonMistakes: Believing Aksum was the first state in the region, when Punt, Yeha and Damat came before it.

g9-history-uh3-t3.summary: Aksum emerged in the first century AD with its nucleus at the city of Aksum and expanded between the fourth and sixth centuries to reach southern Arabia, the Abay, northern Eritrea and north Shewa. Its people lived by plough agriculture, paid tribute and grew rich from trade through Adulis, using minted coins, while Geez developed as a written language. Decline began with the loss of the Red Sea trade after Adulis fell in 702 AD, followed by internal rebellion, the loss of South Arabia and Beja pressure that pushed the state south to Kubar by the ninth century.

g9-history-uh3-t4.overview: The Zagwe dynasty ruled northern Ethiopia from about 1150 to 1270 AD and is remembered for the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela. This lesson explains its Agaw origin, its economy, its architecture and the factors that brought it down.
objectives: Describe the origin and foundation of the Zagwe dynasty
Explain the political and economic features of Zagwe rule
Analyse the architectural achievement of the rock-hewn churches
Evaluate the internal and external factors that caused the fall of Zagwe
Explain how Yekuno Amlak legitimised the Solomonic dynasty
g9-history-uh3-t4.simple: The Zagwe dynasty came from the local Agaw ruling class of Lasta. It was founded around 1150 AD by Mera Tekle Haymnot, who made his capital at Adefa (Roha) in Lasta. Its rise was a shift of political power from the Semitic-speaking Aksumite rulers to the Cushitic-speaking Agaw, not the creation of a new kingdom. The economy rested on agriculture, with trade through the Zeila port and the Dahlak Islands adding income. Zagwe is famous for the eleven monolithic rock-hewn churches built at Roha, later renamed Lalibela, during the reign of Emperor Lalibela in the first half of the thirteenth century. The dynasty fell because of quarrels over succession and opposition from Tigray and Amhara, and in 1270 AD an Amhara chief, Yekuno Amlak, defeated Yetbarek, the last Zagwe king.
g9-history-uh3-t4.detailed:
A political power shift. The Zagwe dynasty came from the local Agaw ruling class in Lasta, part of the Aksumite Empire. It was founded around 1150 AD by Mera Tekle Haymnot, who established a new capital at Adefa (Roha) in Lasta. The founding of the Zagwe dynasty was not the creation of a new kingdom but a shift of political power from the Semitic-speaking Aksumite rulers to the Cushitic-speaking Agaw people.

Economy. The economy of the Zagwe dynasty was based on agriculture, and trade brought additional income to the state. The Zeila port was the main outlet during Zagwe times, while the Dahlak Islands on the Red Sea coast also served as an outlet.

Architecture. The Zagwe dynasty is known in Ethiopian history for its remarkable architectural achievement, the technology of building the monolithic rock-hewn churches at Roha, a capital later renamed Lalibela. The surviving pieces of evidence are the eleven rock-hewn churches constructed during the reign of Emperor Lalibela in the first half of the thirteenth century. These beautiful churches made the town of Lalibela one of the most important centres of learning and Christian culture in Ethiopia, and the expansion of Christianity continued during the Zagwe period (1150-1270).

Opposition and propaganda. Many factors contributed to the downfall of the Zagwe dynasty. The first was the problem of succession to the throne among the Zagwe princes; most of the time they settled this issue by force of arms and could not arrange a smooth succession. Secondly, there was strong opposition to the Zagwe kings throughout their rule, coming from the regions of Tigray and Amhara. In Tigray especially, leading clergy of the churches of Aksum and Debre Damo spread anti-Zagwe propaganda based on the legend of the Queen of Sheba and King Solomon of Israel, so the Zagwe kings were seen as illegitimate successors of Aksum.

The fall of Zagwe. Although the opposition was strongest in Tigray, the initiative to overthrow the Zagwe came from the Amhara region, which lay to the south of Lasta around southern Wollo and northern Shewa. An Amhara chief, Yekuno Amlak, organised a movement against Zagwe rule and defeated Yetbarek, the last Zagwe king, on the battlefield in 1270 AD.

The Solomonic claim. Yekuno Amlak (r. 1270-1285) then declared himself Emperor and became the restorer of the so-called Solomonic dynasty. He established a genealogy that made him a descendant of the last Aksumite king, Dil Naod, who had been deposed by the Zagwe around 1150 AD. Yekuno Amlak and his successors used the legend as an ideological arm to legitimise their political power, and this tradition of identifying the Christian kings of Ethiopia with ancient Israel continued until 1974.

workedExamples.problem: Was the founding of the Zagwe dynasty the start of a new kingdom? Explain.
workedExamples.given: The Zagwe came from the Agaw ruling class of Lasta, part of the former Aksumite Empire, and founded a capital at Adefa (Roha) around 1150 AD.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: a change of ruling group within the same territory is a power shift, not the creation of a new kingdom.
workedExamples.substitution: The territory and the Christian highland state continued, but its rulers changed from Semitic-speaking Aksumites to Cushitic-speaking Agaw.
workedExamples.calculation: Since the land and institutions continued while the ruling dynasty changed, the event is a political power shift.
workedExamples.answer: No. It was a shift of political power from the Aksumite rulers to the Cushitic-speaking Agaw, not a new kingdom.

workedExamples.problem: How did the legend of the Queen of Sheba and King Solomon undermine Zagwe rule?
workedExamples.given: Clergy of Aksum and Debre Damo spread anti-Zagwe propaganda using the legend, presenting the Zagwe as illegitimate successors of Aksum.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: political legitimacy can be destroyed by a rival claim to lineage and tradition.
workedExamples.substitution: The legend tied rightful kingship to descent from Aksum and ancient Israel.
workedExamples.calculation: By denying the Zagwe that descent, the legend made their rule appear illegitimate and prepared the ground for a new dynasty.
workedExamples.answer: It denied the Zagwe a legitimate link to Aksum and Israel, weakening their authority and supporting the claim of Yekuno Amlak.

workedExamples.problem: Yekuno Amlak is called a restorer rather than a conqueror of a new dynasty. Justify this using the textbook.
workedExamples.given: Yekuno Amlak defeated Yetbarek in 1270 AD and claimed descent from Dil Naod, the last Aksumite king deposed around 1150 AD.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: a ruler who claims to continue an older line by descent presents himself as a restorer.
workedExamples.substitution: His genealogy linked him to the Aksumite line rather than to the Zagwe.
workedExamples.calculation: Because his claim was to restore the ancient dynasty of Aksum through Dil Naod, he is called the restorer of the Solomonic dynasty.
workedExamples.answer: He restored rather than founded a dynasty: his genealogy claimed the Aksumite line of Dil Naod, and he used it to legitimise his power.

commonMistakes: Thinking the Zagwe dynasty was a completely new kingdom, when it was a shift of power within the old Aksumite lands.
Believing Zagwe rulers were Semitic speakers, when they came from the Cushitic-speaking Agaw.
Placing the rock-hewn churches in Aksum instead of at Roha, later renamed Lalibela.
Saying the dynasty fell only because of an invasion, when succession quarrels and religious opposition were just as important.
Confusing the founder Mera Tekle Haymnot with the emperor Lalibela, who built the churches.
Assuming the initiative to overthrow Zagwe came from Tigray, when it actually came from the Amhara region.

g9-history-uh3-t4.summary: The Zagwe dynasty, founded around 1150 AD by Mera Tekle Haymnot from the Agaw ruling class of Lasta, marked a shift of power from Semitic-speaking Aksumite rulers to Cushitic-speaking Agaw. Its economy rested on agriculture with trade through Zeila and the Dahlak Islands, and it is remembered for the eleven rock-hewn churches of Lalibela. Succession quarrels and opposition from Tigray and Amhara led to its fall, when Yekuno Amlak defeated Yetbarek in 1270 AD and restored the so-called Solomonic dynasty (r. 1270-1285).

g9-history-uh3-t5.overview: After Islam spread from the eighth century, a series of Muslim states grew along the Zeila trade route in the south-east. This lesson covers the sultanate of Shewa, founded in 896 AD, and its successor and rival, the sultanate of Ifat.
objectives: Describe how Muslim states emerged along the Zeila trade route
Explain the foundation and location of the sultanate of Shewa
Analyse the rise of Ifat under the Walasma dynasty
Evaluate the factors that caused the decline of the sultanate of Shewa
Explain why control of the Zeila trade caused conflict with the Christian highland state
g9-history-uh3-t5.simple: After Islam spread from the beginning of the eighth century, Muslim communities and states grew along the trade routes that ran inland from the port of Zeila. Northern Ethiopian trade had declined because of Arab control of the Red Sea and the destruction of Adulis, so Zeila became the main gateway of Islam into the Horn. The first Muslim state was the sultanate of Shewa, founded in 896 AD. Its founders claimed descent from the Makhzunmite clan of southern Arabia, so its dynasty is called the Makhzunmite, and it lay in the hot lowland on the left of the Awash River. Its ruling family quarrelled over power and the state declined. Ifat, founded by Umar Walasma in 1285 AD, became the strongest Muslim sultanate and the main rival of the Christian highland state, largely over control of the Zeila trade.
g9-history-uh3-t5.detailed:
Muslim states along the trade routes. The introduction of Islam to the Horn was followed by the emergence of a series of Muslim states from the ninth century AD. Northern Ethiopian trade declined because of Arab control of the Red Sea and the destruction of Adulis. Thus Zeila, on the coast of the Gulf of Aden, emerged as the primary port for south-eastern Ethiopian trade and became the most crucial gateway for Islam into the Horn of Africa. Several Muslim states were formed along the Zeila trade route, which linked the port with the rich interior.

Foundation of Shewa. After the spread of Islam from the beginning of the eighth century, viable Muslim communities and states had been established at many locations, especially along the main trade routes from Zeila and its many branches penetrating the interior. The first to be established was the sultanate of Shewa in 896 AD. Because its founders claimed descent from the Makhzunmite clan of southern Arabia, the ruling dynasty became known as the Makhzunmite dynasty.

Location and setting. The sultanate of Shewa was located in the hot lowland region on the left of the Awash River. Its position on the trade routes gave it access to the commerce of the interior, but the ruling family of the state had an internal power struggle which later led to its final decline.

The rise of Ifat. Ifat emerged to the south of Shewa, founded by Umar Walasma, and hence its ruling house is known as the Walasma dynasty; it was established in 1285 AD. Ifat would have destroyed the older Makhzumite dynasty, but instead it became the strongest Muslim sultanate in the region. It controlled a vast territory through which the long-distance trade routes of Zeila passed, so most of the profitable Zeila trade came under the control of Ifat. Eventually, Ifat became the strongest rival of the Christian highland state.

Rivalry with the Christian highland state. Since 1270 the Christian highland state had also developed a great interest in the Zeila trade and trade routes. Therefore the need to control the Zeila trade became the main source of conflict between the two states. This rivalry shaped the politics of the region after the thirteenth century, as the wealth of the interior depended on who controlled the routes that reached the sea.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why the sultanate of Shewa grew where it did.
workedExamples.given: Shewa was founded in 896 AD in the hot lowland on the left of the Awash River, along the main trade routes from Zeila.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: states on a trade route grow where they can tax and control the movement of goods.
workedExamples.substitution: Zeila linked the coast to the rich interior, and Shewa sat on its routes.
workedExamples.calculation: Its position allowed Shewa to draw income from the trade passing between Zeila and the interior, which is why the state grew there.
workedExamples.answer: It grew on the Zeila trade route in the Awash lowlands, where it could profit from trade between the coast and the interior.

workedExamples.problem: Compare the foundation of the sultanate of Shewa and the sultanate of Ifat.
workedExamples.given: Shewa was established in 896 AD by founders claiming descent from the Makhzunmite clan of southern Arabia; Ifat was founded by Umar Walasma in 1285 AD, beginning the Walasma dynasty.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: compare states by date of foundation, ruling dynasty and the claim that legitimised their rule.
workedExamples.substitution: Shewa is older and Makhzunmite; Ifat is later and Walasma.
workedExamples.calculation: Shewa came first, in 896 AD, under the Makhzunmite dynasty, while Ifat followed in 1285 AD under the Walasma dynasty.
workedExamples.answer: Shewa was the earlier state (896 AD, Makhzunmite); Ifat was founded later (1285 AD) by Umar Walasma and became the stronger sultanate.

workedExamples.problem: Why did conflict arise between Ifat and the Christian highland state after 1270?
workedExamples.given: Ifat controlled most of the profitable Zeila trade, and after 1270 the Christian highland state also took a great interest in the Zeila trade and routes.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: two states compete when both depend on controlling the same economic resource.
workedExamples.substitution: The shared resource was the Zeila trade and its routes.
workedExamples.calculation: Because both wanted the income from Zeila, control of the route became the main source of conflict between them.
workedExamples.answer: Both states wanted the wealth of the Zeila trade, so control of its routes became the main source of conflict between them.

commonMistakes: Believing Ifat destroyed the sultanate of Shewa, when Shewa declined mainly through an internal power struggle.
Placing the sultanate of Shewa in the highlands, when it lay in the hot lowland on the left of the Awash River.
Confusing the Makhzunmite dynasty of Shewa with the Walasma dynasty of Ifat.
Thinking Zeila was an Ethiopian interior town, when it was a port on the Gulf of Aden.
Assuming the Christian highland state ignored Zeila, when after 1270 it also wanted to control that trade.
Getting the dates wrong: Shewa 896 AD and Ifat 1285 AD.
applications: Marking the port of Zeila and the Awash River on a map of the Horn.
Explaining in a paragraph how the destruction of Adulis helped Zeila to grow.
Debating why control of trade routes so often causes conflict between states.
Comparing Muslim sultanates and the Christian highland kingdom using a table of features.

g9-history-uh3-t5.summary: After Islam spread from the eighth century, Muslim states grew along the Zeila trade route, and the first was the sultanate of Shewa, founded in 896 AD by rulers of the Makhzunmite clan of southern Arabia. Shewa lay in the hot lowland on the left of the Awash River and declined partly because of an internal power struggle. Ifat, founded by Umar Walasma in 1285 AD under the Walasma dynasty, became the strongest Muslim sultanate and the main rival of the Christian highland state, above all over control of the profitable Zeila trade.
